summary: Explains the IP Router Alert Option, which flags a packet so that routers along the path look at it more closely. It discusses the security risks of the option and gives guidelines for protocols that use it, such as RSVP and IGMP. It is a best current practice and updates RFC 2113 and RFC 2711.

eli5.summary: Some letters have a sticker saying "look inside, please". Routers normally rush past packets, but the sticker makes them stop. This document says when stickers are a good idea and how they can be abused.

subtitle: Why the IP Router Alert Option is a denial-of-service risk, and where it can safely be used.

tldr.problem: The IP Router Alert Option tells routers to look more closely at a packet, but routers cannot reliably tell wanted Router Alert packets from unwanted ones, so flooding them can overload the slow path and cause denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends against relying on Router Alert across independent domains in the Internet, describes controlled environments where it is safe, tells service providers to protect themselves, and gives router implementation guidelines.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2113 and RFC 2711 with usage and protection guidance rather than changing the option itself.

today: RFC 6398 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2113 and RFC 2711, which define the IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options.

sections.title: What the Router Alert Option Is
sections.content:
The IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options are defined in RFC 2113 and RFC 2711. Together the RFC calls them the IP Router Alert. It is an IP option that alerts transit routers to more closely examine the contents of a packet.

Several protocols use it, including RSVP, PGM, IGMP, MLD, MRD and GIST. RFC 6398 does not change the option. It discusses security and usage on the basis of the current specifications, and it leaves possible future enhancements, such as one proposal the IETF had not adopted, outside its scope.

It also keeps broader topics out of scope. The IPv6 hop-by-hop options header and IPv4 options in general raise similar concerns, but covering them would need more material.
sections.eli5: A Router Alert is a sticker on a packet that says look at me closely. Normal packets just get waved through, but stickered ones make the router stop and read them.

sections.title: The Security Problem
sections.content:
The RFC defines two paths inside a router. The fast path is the hardware or ASIC route that normally forwards packets. The slow path is a software route for packets needing special processing. Router Alert packets are often sent, or punted, to the slow path. An attacker who floods a router with bogus Router Alert packets can use up a significant share of the slow path and cause drops that hurt every other protocol using it. This results in a denial of service.

The core issue is that the option gives no good way to tell wanted packets from unwanted ones. RFC 2113 offers no way to identify different users, and RFC 2711 only a very limited one. Looking at the next level protocol is too coarse: the same protocol number is used for different applications or contexts, such as RSVP and RSVP-TE, and some protocols ride over TCP or UDP. The Value field does not help much either. Only one value, zero, was defined in RFC 2113, an IANA registry came later, and some implementations reportedly ignore the field. Rate limiting helps only if it is fine-grained enough, otherwise an attack still harms legitimate protocols.

The RFC compares this with BGP peering, whose attack vector is similar or somewhat less serious. BGP peers are pre-identified, the exposure is limited to edge routers, and policy typically stops bad data being re-injected. Even so, it notes that bad BGP security practice and strict edge/core separation not holding can weaken these advantages.
sections.eli5: Imagine if anyone could stick a look at me sticker on a letter and make the mail clerk stop. Someone could stick it on a million letters and the clerk would never get anything else done.

sections.title: Do Not Depend on It End to End
sections.content:
Because of these risks, network operators SHOULD actively protect themselves from externally generated Router Alert packets. In practice they often isolate themselves, either by tunneling the packets so the option is hidden, or by occasional or systematic dropping, for example through rate limiting.

So applications and protocols SHOULD NOT be deployed with a dependency on processing the Router Alert Option, as currently specified, across independent administrative domains in the Internet. The RFC calls the hypothetical end-to-end use the Peer Model, because core routers in different domains would all take part in the same signaling flow.

The RFC adds that the underlying worry is wider than this one option. Operators do not want uncontrolled outside devices tapping into the control plane of their core routers, whether through Router Alert or another means such as deep packet inspection. Cross-domain signaling in a Peer Model is therefore unlikely to be welcomed whether or not it uses Router Alert.
sections.eli5: A town will not let strangers from far away make its mail clerks stop and read letters. So do not build something that needs every town along the way to cooperate.

sections.title: Controlled Environments Where It Is Safe
sections.content:
Router Alert can be used safely where the operator controls who sends it. The RFC describes several cases.

Within one administrative domain, the administrator may know Router Alert packets only come from trusted devices, or may have enough filtering and rate limiting. A private enterprise network firewalled from the Internet and using RSVP reservations for voice and video is an example. Closely cooperating domains that act as one trust domain can also use it. Where untrusted Router Alert packets are encapsulated across a trusted area, as in RFC 6178, a service provider can run RSVP-TE inside.

In an Overlay Model, an enterprise's sites are interconnected through a provider network that protects itself without dropping the packets. In a water-tight overlay, Router Alert packets from the customer network cannot leak into the provider network. In a leak-controlled overlay, they may reach the provider's edge routers, which are protected by rate limiting and filtering, but not its core. The provider's own use of Router Alert, such as RSVP-TE, can run at the same time.
sections.eli5: Stickers are fine inside a school or office where everybody is known and trusted. The trouble only starts when strangers from outside can use them.

sections.title: What Service Providers Should Do
sections.content:
A service provider MUST implement strong protection of its network against Router Alert attacks. It SHOULD use mechanisms that avoid, or at least minimise, dropping end-to-end Router Alert packets other than those involved in an attack, so customers can still use overlay deployments.

The RFC gives examples. A provider that runs no protocol depending on Router Alert might simply turn off punting of such packets, letting them transit safely. A provider that does run one, such as RSVP-TE, can use selective filtering and rate limiting, and can reduce its reliance on the option with protocol features such as RSVP refresh reduction (RFC 2961). It can also use tunneling as in RFC 6178. The RFC says tunneling over an MPLS backbone is well understood, while tunneling over a non-MPLS IP backbone raises issues and is not common practice at the time of writing.

As a last resort a provider with no safe option can drop the packets, but that blocks users from deploying valid applications on top of its network.
sections.eli5: The post office has to protect itself from sticker floods. It is best to do that without throwing away every stickered letter, but if it has no other way, it may have to.

sections.title: Guidelines for Router Implementers
sections.content:
A router implementation SHOULD include protections against Router Alert based denial-of-service attacks that suit its target environments. New implementations MAY add selective, possibly dynamic, filtering and rate limiting. Edge routers may tunnel received packets over the core as in RFC 6178.

Implementations SHOULD offer a configuration option to simply ignore Router Alert in IPv4 and IPv6 packets. That lets the packets cross a network segment safely, as long as the operator never uses them there.

If a packet carries Router Alert but its next level protocol is not one the router cares about, RFC 2113 does not say what to do. Following the implied behaviour, a router SHOULD forward such a packet in the fast path, subject to normal policy, rather than punt it. Not punting protects the router, and forwarding keeps end-to-end transport transparent. An implementation MAY also choose between forwarding and punting based on the Value field.

The security considerations section only says that the document expands those of RFC 2113 and RFC 2711, and points to RFC 4081 for more.
sections.eli5: A smart mail clerk should ignore stickers on letters about things the clerk does not handle, and just send them on quickly. It should also have a switch for ignoring stickers entirely.
